To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

170 drugs or drug groups were significantly associated with cancer incidence, 57 were significantly inversely associated with cancer incidence; 227 of 1,500 possible associations were significant; 170 positive, and 57 negative, associations were statistically significant; and the most notable finding was the association of several antibiotics with lung cancer.
there were 227 statistically signficant associations between 215 drugs or groups and cancer, 170 positive and 57 negative.

there is little evidence of an association of most commonly used prescription medications with cancer incidence, that there is suggestive evidence for a link between antibiotics, both oral (especially erythromycin) and topical (especially tetracycline and erythromycin), and lung cancer, and that our study design is not powerful enough to detect moderate increases (relative risk = 1.3 to 1.6) in cancer incidence associated with use of drugs that are not commonly used.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying and quantifying associations between prescription drugs and cancer.
the possible role of medications in cancer causation.
the identification of drugs that might be carcinogenic, and with the identification of factors that might modify the carcinogenic effects of drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of our study are consistent with the hypothesis that prescription drug use does not substantially increase risk of cancer, but that the hypothesis is not conclusively supported.
, in this study, the drugs tested were not associated with increased cancer risk, with a few notable exceptions.

, for this population, there is no evidence of substantial carcinogenic effects of prescription drugs in general, but that there may be a need for further studies and continued follow-up of certain drugs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most common drugs used in the 1969-73 period did not appear to be carcinogenic, but some less common drugs might have carcinogenic potential and should be studied more carefully.
most drugs do not appear to increase cancer risk, but that some drugs, including some antibiotics, should be studied further.
the most important findings were the negative ones, indicating the absence of major effects on cancer incidence of most of the commonly prescribed medications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in general, prescription medications are safe.
the use of computerized pharmacy records to identify possible carcinogens in prescription medications has proved to be a valuable approach.

the use of computerized databases to screen for associations between medications and cancer incidence has the potential to generate testable hypotheses and identify areas for further study, and that such studies can be carried out in large health care organizations with minimal cost and effort.
